claims.text: Uniform single-phase formation of noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by synchronization of precursor reduction kinetics under conditions of limited atomic mobility.
Matching the reduction rates of the different noble-metal precursors produces stochastic nucleation and a well-mixed alloy.
Unsynchronized reduction promotes sequential nucleation and phase segregation.
The relevant starting material can be a crystalline single-source precursor in which Pt, Ir, Rh, Os, and Ru complexes are mixed locally.
Low-temperature reduction of a solid mixed precursor limits free atomic mobility.
The unchanged synthesis has inherent differences among the reduction rates of its individual metal precursors.
Constrained atomic mobility inhibits long-range diffusion during particle formation.
Constrained mobility enforces stochastic, local nucleation after reduction is triggered.
Synchronizing all precursor reductions induces simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous nucleation promotes random statistical incorporation of every element type into each nanoparticle.
Synchronizing reduction minimizes sequential reduction and subsequent phase segregation.
Relative to the unchanged baseline, kinetic synchronization will produce a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
Relative to the unchanged baseline, kinetic synchronization will reduce phase separation.
Relative to the unchanged baseline, kinetic synchronization will narrow the nanoparticle size distribution.
In the five-element baseline, inherent reduction-rate differences lead to sequential reduction and therefore phase-segregated, compositionally inhomogeneous nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism should apply to low-temperature reductions of solid, mixed precursors with limited atomic mobility.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when high temperature or other conditions that enhance atomic mobility dominate particle formation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and baseline treat synchronized reduction as governing single-phase five-element HEA formation and imply that consecutive reduction causes segregation, whereas the cited five-element conclusion states that single-phase HEA particles formed even when the elements reduced consecutively. The synchronization rule in the evidence is established for binary alloys, not for the five-element system.
